notes.meaning: David returned to the ruins of Ziklag after defeating the Amalekite raiders, staying there for two days. While he waited, he showed patience rather than rushing to claim the kingdom. He trusted God's timing and did not try to speed up Saul's downfall.

On the third day, a messenger came from Saul's army with torn clothes and dirt on his head, which were traditional signs of deep mourning. When he reached David, he fell to the ground to show great honor. He treated David as the rising king, hoping to receive a personal reward.
David asked the young man where he had come from. The man answered that he had just escaped with his life from the camp of Israel.

David asked for a report of the battle, eager to know how the nation had fared. The messenger told him that the army had fled in defeat, many soldiers were dead, and both King Saul and his son Jonathan had been killed.

David asked the young man how he could be so sure about the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. Because this was huge news that would change the whole nation, David wanted certain proof before taking any action.

The young man said he happened to be on Mount Gilboa, where he saw Saul leaning heavily on his spear as enemy chariots and horsemen closed in. Most commentators believe the man made up this story to gain favor with David, since Saul had already fallen on his own sword.
The messenger claimed that Saul looked behind him, saw him, and called out. When Saul asked who he was, the man told him he was an Amalekite, a member of a long-time enemy nation of Israel.
According to the messenger, Saul begged the stranger to stand over him and finish his life. Saul claimed that agony and weakness had seized him, even though his life was still lingering in his body.

The man stated that he killed Saul because he was sure the wounded king could not survive anyway. He took the royal crown and armlet from Saul's body and brought them to David to prove the death and claim a reward.

Instead of rejoicing over his enemy's death, David tore his clothes in grief, and all his men did the same. They spent the rest of the day weeping, mourning, and fasting for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen soldiers of God's people. This showed that David truly loved his nation and held no hatred in his heart toward Saul.
David questioned the messenger again about his origin, acting like a careful judge in a courtroom. The man confirmed that he was the son of an Amalekite who was living as an immigrant in Israel.

David asked the young man why he was not terrified to raise his hand against the Lord's anointed king. David had spared Saul's life multiple times because he believed only God had the authority to remove a ruler He had chosen.

David ordered one of his soldiers to strike down the Amalekite immediately. David declared that the man had brought death on himself, because his own confession proved him guilty of treason against God's appointed king. Whether his tale was true or a greedy lie, the messenger condemned himself with his own words.

David composed a sorrowful funeral song for Saul and Jonathan and ordered the people of Judah to learn it. The song was titled 'The Bow,' honoring Jonathan's weapon of war and the skill of Israelite archers. It was recorded in the Book of Jashar, an ancient collection of Hebrew historical songs.

David opened his poem by calling Saul and Jonathan the beauty and glory of Israel, now lying dead on the heights of Gilboa. He introduced the repeated refrain that echoes throughout the lament: 'How the mighty have fallen!' In his deep sorrow, David focused on the honor of the leaders rather than their past mistakes.

David pleaded that the news not be spoken in Philistine cities like Gath or Ashkelon. He could not stand the thought of pagan women dancing and celebrating over the defeat of God's covenant people. His greatest concern was that God's name and people would be mocked.

In poetic grief, David called on the mountains of Gilboa to have no dew, no rain, and no fertile fields for offerings. He spoke this curse because the shields of Israel's brave soldiers had been cast away and defiled with blood. Saul's shield lay discarded as though it had never been anointed and prepared for battle.

David celebrated the fierce fighting skills of Saul and Jonathan in their earlier battles. Jonathan's bow never retreated, and Saul's sword always struck its targets among the enemy warriors. Remembering their past victories made their sudden fall all the more tragic.

David praised Saul and Jonathan as beloved and delightful in life, noting that they were not separated even in death. Jonathan remained loyal to his father to the very end, and both fought with the swiftness of eagles and the strength of lions. David generously remembered what was noble and loving about them.

David called on the women of Israel to weep for King Saul, who had brought prosperity and rich spoils from his military victories. Under his rule, they had received luxurious scarlet clothing and gold ornaments to wear. David reminded the nation of the good years and security Saul had provided.

David repeated the mournful chorus that the mighty soldiers had fallen in the thick of the fight. He turned his grief directly toward Jonathan, weeping that his dearest companion was slain upon the hills.

David poured out his broken heart for Jonathan, calling him his brother and remembering how delightful their friendship had been. Jonathan had shown extraordinary, selfless loyalty by standing with David even when it meant giving up his own claim to the throne. David valued this loyal covenant friendship more than the deepest human affection he had ever known.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims translation includes an additional line comparing David's affection to a mother's love for her only child.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern readers view the relationship between David and Jonathan as romantic, but commentators explain that the Hebrew language describes deep, selfless friendship and covenant loyalty.

notes.meaning: The funeral poem ends with one last sigh of grief for Israel's leaders. David mourned that the mighty warriors had fallen and the nation's weapons of war had perished with them.
